name: ctxdiff
description: Find what breaks your LLM agent's prompt cache and wastes its context — git diff for the context window. A local-first context-window debugger for LLM agents. Wrap your OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock client in one line and record every call's context into a shareable .ctrace, then diff turns, profile prompt-cache breaks, and open a self-contained HTML dashboard. Cross-compatible with the Python ctxdiff SDK.
author: Salman Zafar (https://salmanzafar.dev)
//gpt-tokenizer: PINNED TO AN EXACT VERSION, ON PURPOSE - do not restore the ^ caret.

ctxdiff ships two SDKs (npm `ctxdiff`, PyPI `ctxdiff`) that promise the same trace renders to the same numbers in both. They get those numbers from two INDEPENDENT reimplementations of the same o200k_base BPE table - gpt-tokenizer here, tiktoken in ../pyproject.toml - on independent release cadences. A .ctrace itself is safe either way (a block's content hash is sha256 over role + kind + text; token counts are NOT hashed), but every rendered number is downstream of a token count, so the day the two libraries disagree on one encoding, `ctxdiff tokens`, the cache profiler's re-billed totals and the HTML dashboard's percentages diverge between the SDKs. A caret range lets `npm install` in a fresh clone pull a newer minor that changes published numbers with no ctxdiff commit behind it - invisible until a user reports it.

TO RE-PIN (a deliberate, reviewable act - never a drive-by bump): 1. bump this version AND `tiktoken` in ../pyproject.toml (keep the two libraries' encodings in step; re-pinning one alone is what drift IS), 2. update tokenizers.*.pinned_version in ../spec/golden/manifest.json, 3. run `npm run golden:regen` (or `python spec/golden/regenerate.py` from the repo root) - it rewrites the committed expectations AND cross-checks that both SDKs reproduce them, 4. review the diff under spec/golden/expected/. An EMPTY diff means the tokenizers still agree with the previous release. A non-empty diff is the tokenizer changing its mind about real text: understand which encoding moved before merging it.
